newsitem.title: USA: Blacks rejected twice as often for U.S. home loans.
newsitem.headline: Blacks rejected twice as often for U.S. home loans.

text.p: Black Americans remained twice as likely as whites to be turned down for a home-mortgage loan last year, a study said Monday.
Asian Americans were least likely of any racial or ethnic group to be rejected.

The findings were contained in a report released by the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council, an umbrella group for five federal regulatory agencies that examined lending activity at 9,300 banks and other lending institutions subject to federal rules on mortgage lending.
The pattern of rejections was little changed from recent years, notwithstanding a drive by banking regulators since the start of the Clinton administration to toughly enforce fair-lending rules.

Last year, banks, savings institutions, credit unions and mortgage companies turned down 48.8 percent of applications for mortgage loans received from blacks and 24.1 percent from whites -- a 2-1 ratio. That was virtually the same ratio as in 1995 when 40.5 percent of black and 20.6 percent of white applicants were rejected.
The rejection rate for Asian Americans was markedly lower, with 13.8 percent of applicants denied loans in 1996 and 12.5 percent turned down in 1995.

For Hispanic applicants, the rejection rate in 1996 was 34.4 percent compared with 29.5 percent in 1995. Native American applicants were turned down in 50.2 percent of cases in 1996, up from 41.4 percent in 1995.
Roughly 15 million loans and applications were examined in the latest study, up about 33 percent from 1995.
Poor credit or no credit history were most frequently cited as reasons for denying loan applications.

A spokeswoman for the American Bankers' Association said the higher volume of applications reflected "the continuing outreach that bankers have been doing to reach under-served markets" and said that should eventually mean lower rejection rates for minorities because they were receiving more counselling in how to qualify and to apply.
"We would hope that increased outreach and sensitivity to the markets that we are trying to serve would mean more successful applicants in future," the spokeswoman said.

The study said lending to lower-income households rose "somewhat more" than lending to higher-income households in 1996 and that government-backed and conventional mortgage loans to all racial and ethnic groups increased from 1995.

Lending to borrowers who earned less than 80 percent of median income in their region rose 13 percent in 1996, while lending to wealthier households rose 12 percent last year after falling 2 percent in 1995.
Eugene Ludwig, Comptroller of the Currency, said in a statement there were some promising developments in the latest report.

"Many of the trends are positive, with lending to lower-income households up more than lending to higher-income households," Ludwig said. "However, some of the data show a need for more detailed analysis."
